feedback: Target kits: hot-and-sunny → sun hat, sunscreen, t-shirt, water (not a heavy coat); cold-and-snowy → warm coat, gloves, scarf; rainy → umbrella and wellies/waterproofs.

If the child picks favourite or identical items across different cards, prompt the consequence: 'What will happen to you outside dressed like that in the snow?' to reconnect the choice to the weather.
If the child adds warm layers for hot sun, link clothing to comfort and safety: ask how they'd feel running in a thick coat in the sun.

If the child chooses nothing for strong sun ('it's nice out, I don't need anything'), introduce sun protection as active preparation: a hat and sunscreen are the hot-sun kit, just as a coat is the cold kit.
activities.intendedInsight: A child who can assemble a sensible, condition-matched kit for several different conditions — and explain the choices — has connected weather observation to everyday preparation.
learnerActions: Lay out a mix of real or pictured clothing and equipment: sun hat, sunscreen, warm coat, gloves, scarf, umbrella, wellies, t-shirt, water bottle.
Draw three weather cards: hot-and-sunny, cold-and-snowy, rainy.
For each card, get a doll (or yourself) ready to go outside by choosing the right items, and act it out (e.g. actually put the coat on for the cold card).
Say why each item suits that weather.
Link it to the day: 'How does this weather change what we can do at playtime or walking to school?'
activities.title: Get ready for real weather cards (performance task)

feedback: Accept any reason that tracks the weather: 'the umbrella keeps the rain off me', 'the hat shades my eyes and skin'.
If a reason is missing, prompt for it — matching without a reason only meets half the goal.
Reinforce sun protection as a real answer for the hot-sun case, not an optional extra.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can pair conditions with appropriate gear and give a short reason for each pairing.
learnerActions: Match each weather to its gear: rain → coat + umbrella; hot sun → sun hat + sunscreen; cold → hat + gloves + layers; wind → windproof.
For each match, answer a 'why do we wear this?' question in your own words.
Try a choice question such as 'What should you wear on a hot sunny day, and why not a woolly jumper?'
activities.title: Match weather to gear and say why

feedback: Draw out the reason, not just the item: if the child names a coat, ask what the coat does for them.
If the child says sun needs no preparation, gently surface overheating and sunburn as reasons to prepare for strong sun too.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the reasons into words strengthens the justification behind each clothing choice.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as 'It's raining out — what should I wear, and why?'
Explain why the umbrella is needed on the rainy day, and why a sun hat and sunscreen are the main things to choose on the sunny day.
Say what could happen on a hot, sunny day if you went out with no hat and no sunscreen.
activities.title: Talk it through: why this, not that?
